V.1.title: Two marriages
V.1.reflection: Confucius gives his daughter in marriage to Gongye Chang, who had been in prison though not guilty, and his niece to Nan Rong, a man who would keep office in good times and avoid punishment in bad. The book records these as judgements of character. The chapter belongs to a world where a father or uncle arranged a marriage, and it reads as such.
V.1.question: What would you want to know about a person before trusting them with someone you love?

V.2.title: Where did he learn it?
V.2.reflection: Confucius praises Zijian as a junzi, and then asks: if Lu had no junzi, where could he have acquired this? Character is learned from those around us. The praise of one person is also praise of a place.
V.2.question: From whom, around you, did you take the qualities you are proudest of?

V.3.title: A jade vessel
V.3.reflection: Zigong asks what the Master thinks of him. "You are a vessel." Which kind? "A sacrificial vessel of jade." After II.12, that the junzi is not a vessel, the answer is both praise and limit: precious and fine, and still made for a purpose.
V.3.question: If someone you respect described you as a vessel, which kind would they name?

V.4.title: No need for a ready tongue
V.4.reflection: Someone remarks that Ran Yong is good but not eloquent. What use is a ready tongue, Confucius answers; quick retorts mostly earn dislike. Whether Yong is fully ren he does not know, but eloquence is beside the point.
V.4.question: Do you value quick speech in others more than it deserves?

V.5.title: Not yet confident
V.5.reflection: Confucius urges Qidiao Kai to take office, and Kai replies that he does not yet trust himself in it. The Master is pleased. Knowing that one is not ready is itself a kind of readiness.
V.5.question: What are you not yet ready for, and how do you know?

V.6.title: On a raft, out to sea
V.6.reflection: My Way does not go forward, Confucius says; I will take a raft and float out to sea, and Zilu would come with me. Zilu is delighted. The Master adds that Zilu loves daring more than he does. Legge reads the last words as a lack of judgement; others read them as "there is nowhere to get the timber". Either way, a moment of discouragement turns into gentle teasing.
V.6.question: Who would follow you onto the raft, and would you want them to?

V.7.title: Capable, but is he ren?
V.7.reflection: Meng Wu asks whether Zilu, Ran Qiu and Gongxi Chi are humane. Confucius describes each one's ability exactly, an army, a town, a court reception, and each time says he does not know if they are ren. Talent is easy to name; goodness he will not grant on demand.
V.7.question: Could you describe what someone is good at without being able to say whether they are good?

V.8.title: Neither of us equals Hui
V.8.reflection: Confucius asks Zigong whether he or Hui is better. How could I compare, says Zigong: Hui hears one thing and knows ten, I hear one and know two. The Master agrees, and in the Chinese adds that neither of them, he included, is equal to Hui. Legge reads it as "I grant you"; many others read "you and I are not equal to him".
V.8.question: Whom do you admire without envy, and what makes that possible?

V.9.title: Rotten wood
V.9.reflection: Zai Yu sleeps during the day, and Confucius says rotten wood cannot be carved, nor a dung wall plastered. Then a second remark: he used to hear people's words and trust their conduct; now he hears their words and watches their conduct. Zai Yu taught him this. The harshest rebuke in the book ends in a lesson the teacher learned.
V.9.question: Whose actions taught you to stop relying on their words?

V.10.title: No one unbending
V.10.reflection: Confucius has never seen a truly steadfast person. Someone names Shen Cheng. But Cheng has desires, the Master answers; how could he be unbending? Firmness, in this sense, is freedom from being pulled by wants.
V.10.question: What wants most easily bend your resolve?

V.11.title: Not yet within reach
V.11.reflection: Zigong says that what he does not want others to do to him, he does not want to do to them. Confucius: Ci, this is not yet within your reach. The rule is stated perfectly and the Master answers that stating it is not the same as living it. The thought returns in XII.2 and XV.23.
V.11.question: Which principle do you state easily that you have not yet reached?

V.12.title: What could not be heard
V.12.reflection: Zigong says the Master's culture and conduct could be learned from him, but his words on human nature and the Way of Heaven could not be heard. Either he rarely spoke of them, or they could not be grasped by hearing. The chapter marks the edge of what the disciples received.
V.12.question: What did a teacher of yours teach by example that they never put into words?

V.13.title: Afraid to hear more
V.13.reflection: When Zilu heard something he had not yet been able to put into practice, he was only afraid of hearing something else. The impatient disciple has here a virtue: he does not let learning outrun doing.
V.13.question: What have you learned recently that you have not yet put into practice?

V.14.title: Not ashamed to ask
V.14.reflection: Why was Kong Wenzi given the posthumous name Wen, "cultured"? Because he was quick and loved learning, and was not ashamed to ask those beneath him. The title honours a habit, not an achievement.
V.14.question: Whom below you in some ranking could you learn from, if you asked?

V.15.title: Four ways of Zichan
V.15.reflection: Zichan, the great minister of Zheng, had four marks of the junzi: humble in his own conduct, respectful to superiors, kind in caring for the people, just in employing them. The list looks in four directions, self, above, below, and the tasks given to others.
V.15.question: In which of the four directions are you weakest?

V.16.title: Respect that lasts
V.16.reflection: Yan Ping knew how to keep friendships: however long he knew someone, he showed them the same respect as at first. Familiarity did not wear the courtesy down.
V.16.question: With whom has long acquaintance worn away your first respect?

V.17.title: A house for a tortoise
V.17.reflection: Zang Wenzhong kept a great divining tortoise in a house decorated with carved hills and painted water plants, ornaments fit for a ruler's temple. How can that be called wisdom? He was famed as wise, and Confucius notes where he was not.
V.17.question: What lavish habit undermines a reputation you otherwise deserve?

V.18.title: Loyal, pure, not yet ren
V.18.reflection: Zizhang asks about two officials: one who took and left office without joy or resentment and briefed his successor; one who abandoned his wealth rather than serve a regicide. Confucius calls the first loyal and the second pure, and of each says he does not know how they could be called ren. Fine single virtues do not add up to the whole.
V.18.question: Is there a single virtue you have that you mistake for the whole of goodness?

V.19.title: Twice is enough
V.19.reflection: Ji Wenzi thought three times before acting. Confucius, hearing it, says twice will do. Reflection has a measure too: past a point it becomes hesitation.
V.19.question: What decision are you thinking over a third time?

V.20.title: The wisdom of seeming foolish
V.20.reflection: When his state had the Way, Ning Wuzi was wise; when it lost the Way, he played the fool. His wisdom can be equalled, his foolishness cannot. In a dangerous court, appearing harmless can be the harder art.
V.20.question: When is it wiser to seem less clever than you are?

V.21.title: Let me go home
V.21.reflection: Travelling in Chen, Confucius exclaims: let me return! The young men of my school are ambitious and hasty, they have finished patterns but do not know how to cut them. He longs to shape them. A teacher abroad thinks of his students.
V.21.question: What work at home do you miss when you are away from it?

V.22.title: Not keeping old grudges
V.22.reflection: Bo Yi and Shu Qi, the two brothers who starved rather than serve a conqueror, did not keep old wrongs in mind, and so there was little resentment. Holding grudges keeps resentment alive on both sides.
V.22.question: What old wrong are you still keeping?

V.23.title: The borrowed vinegar
V.23.reflection: Who says Weisheng Gao is upright? Someone asked him for vinegar, and rather than say he had none, he begged some from a neighbour and handed it over as his own. A small vanity becomes a small dishonesty.
V.23.question: When have you pretended to have something you had to borrow?

V.24.title: What I am ashamed of
V.24.reflection: Fine words, an ingratiating face, excessive deference: Zuo Qiuming was ashamed of them, and so is Confucius. Hiding resentment and befriending the person: the same. Shame here is a compass, pointing at insincerity.
V.24.question: Is there someone you treat as a friend while hiding resentment?

V.25.title: Each one's wishes
V.25.reflection: Confucius asks Yan Hui and Zilu for their wishes. Zilu would share his carriages and furs with friends without minding the wear. Hui would not boast of his goodness or display his merits. Asked in turn, the Master wishes rest for the old, good faith with friends, and tender care for the young.
V.25.question: If asked for your wishes in one sentence, what would you say?

V.26.title: Accusing oneself
V.26.reflection: It is hopeless, Confucius says; he has never seen anyone who could see his own faults and accuse himself inwardly. The chapter is a sigh. It also names the practice it says is missing.
V.26.question: When did you last see a fault of your own clearly, without excuse?

V.27.title: Love of learning
V.27.reflection: In a hamlet of ten households there must be someone as loyal and trustworthy as I am, Confucius says, but not one who loves learning as I do. He claims little for his virtue and much for his appetite to learn.
V.27.question: What do you love learning about, more than most people around you?
